content: The World Health Organization (WHO) South-East Asia Region has developed sodium benchmarks for packaged foods as of September 2023. These benchmarks aim to address the rising sodium intake from packaged foods in the region, which is contributing to significant public health concerns. The benchmarks were created to guide countries in setting sodium reduction targets for packaged foods, with the ultimate goal of reducing population sodium intake and improving health outcomes. The sodium benchmarks were developed through a collaborative process coordinated by the Nutrition and Health for Development Unit of the WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia. Technical work was conducted by experts from institutions such as The George Institute for Global Health in Australia and Wageningen University & Research in the Netherlands. National experts and WHO country offices also contributed by providing data, validation, and feedback on sodium intake and packaged food consumption in the region. The increasing consumption of packaged foods in the South-East Asia Region has necessitated the introduction of food policies aimed at reducing sodium content in these products. Sodium benchmarks for each food category were selected based on the lowest maximum values from existing national or regional targets. While the global sodium benchmarks provide guidance, they do not comprehensively account for the specific foods consumed or the current sodium levels in packaged foods in the region. Therefore, the benchmarks were reviewed and tailored to include region-specific sources of sodium and to ensure their appropriateness for the South-East Asia Region. The purpose of adapting the global sodium benchmarks is to support countries in the region in adopting sodium reformulation targets, accelerating the target-setting process, and promoting the reformulation of products to lower sodium content. This approach ensures that future targets are feasible and result in meaningful reductions in population sodium intake. Adjustments were made, and additional benchmarks were established where necessary, to reflect the unique dietary patterns and sodium sources in the region. Sodium reformulation benchmarks offer several advantages over other policies, such as front-of-pack labeling (FoPL). While FoPL focuses on multiple nutrients, sodium reformulation benchmarks specifically target sodium reduction in high-sodium food categories. This category-specific approach is more effective in motivating food companies to reduce sodium levels in their products. Additionally, sodium reformulation benchmarks are likely to have a more equitable impact, as they affect the entire food supply and all consumers, regardless of socioeconomic status or education level. The methodology for reviewing the suitability of the global sodium benchmarks and setting regional benchmarks involved several steps. Data on the main food category sources of sodium were collected, considering both the quantity of food consumed and the sodium content of these products. Products with high sodium levels, such as seasoning powders, and those consumed in large quantities, such as bread, were prioritized. The data were verified by regional experts, and missing information was identified. Opinions on priority food categories for sodium reformulation were also gathered. Using the available data, sodium benchmarks were established for priority food categories. Products were categorized into existing food categories in the global sodium benchmarks, and any products not covered were assigned to the most similar category. The categorization was independently checked by researchers, and the dataset was cleaned to remove products with missing or implausible sodium content data. The suitability of the sodium benchmark levels was reviewed by comparing them against the current sodium content of products sold in the region. If a significant proportion of products met the global benchmark, it was deemed feasible and adopted without changes. If less than one-third of products met the benchmark, higher interim sodium targets were developed to allow for gradual reduction over time. Conversely, if more than two-thirds of products already met the benchmark, stricter sodium targets were planned to drive further reduction. Interim sodium targets were set based on the sodium content levels of existing products in the region and corroborated by targets from other countries, where available. Depending on the distribution of sodium content, targets were set at either the 33rd or 50th percentile (median) sodium content levels. A threeto four-year timeframe was recommended for achieving these targets, allowing for gradual reformulation and ensuring feasibility for food companies and acceptability to the public. The sodium benchmarks were tailored to the South-East Asia Region to address the specific dietary patterns and sodium sources in the region. Six priority food categories were identified for sodium reformulation: meat and meat products, fish and fish products, spices, sauces, and seasonings, ready-to-eat savories (snacks), instant noodles, and breads and bakery wares. These categories were selected based on their contribution to sodium intake and their potential for reformulation. The benchmarks aim to drive progress in sodium reduction, promote healthier food environments, and ultimately improve public health outcomes in the South-East Asia Region.
